title: Royal Crest Maths: Newton's apples, what is x? and Crest Slate
_note: say = text sent to ElevenLabs (maths in words); cap = on-screen caption (maths in symbols).

lines.say: England, sixteen sixty-six. Isaac Newton is twenty-three, reading in his mother's garden.
lines.cap: England, 1666. Isaac Newton is 23, reading in his mother’s garden.

lines.say: And then... an apple falls.
lines.cap: And then… an apple falls.

lines.say: Hold on. Did it hit him on the head?
lines.cap: Hold on. Did it hit him on the head?

lines.say: No! That part is a myth. But it made him ask a question nobody had answered: why do apples always fall straight down?
lines.cap: No! That part is a myth. But it made him ask a question nobody had answered: why do apples always fall straight down?

lines.say: He picked it up, and started to think in numbers. That question led him to gravity, and to some of the most powerful maths ever written.
lines.cap: He picked it up, and started to think in numbers. That question led him to gravity, and to some of the most powerful maths ever written.

lines.say: So today, we start where every great mathematician starts: with a mystery number.
lines.cap: So today, we start where every great mathematician starts: with a mystery number.

lines.say: Newton's apples. What is x?
lines.cap: Newton’s apples. What is x?

lines.say: Here is Newton's basket. There are some apples inside, but the lid is closed.
lines.cap: Here is Newton’s basket. There are some apples inside, but the lid is closed.

lines.say: So how many apples are in there?
lines.cap: So how many apples are in there?

lines.say: We don't know yet. So we give that number a name. We call it x.
lines.cap: We don’t know yet. So we give that number a name. We call it x.

lines.say: x is a variable: a number we don't know yet. Like a basket, waiting to be opened.
lines.cap: x is a variable: a number we don’t know yet. Like a basket, waiting to be opened.

lines.say: Let's find it. On this side of the scale: three apples, and the basket.
lines.cap: Let’s find it. On this side of the scale: three apples, and the basket.

lines.say: On the other side: seven apples. And the scale balances.
lines.cap: On the other side: seven apples. And the scale balances.

lines.say: So three plus x equals seven.
Yes. Whatever we do to one side, we do to the other. Take three apples off both sides.
lines.cap: Yes. Whatever we do to one side, we do to the other. Take 3 apples off both sides.

lines.say: The scale still balances. The basket equals four apples. x equals four!
lines.cap: The scale still balances. The basket equals 4 apples. x = 4!

lines.say: Open it! Four apples. Newton, you're a genius.
lines.cap: Open it! Four apples. Newton, you’re a genius.

lines.say: Now, every basket holds the same number of apples: x.
lines.cap: Now, every basket holds the same number of apples: x.

lines.say: Two baskets plus three baskets is five baskets. Two x plus three x is five x.
lines.cap: Two baskets plus three baskets is five baskets. 2x + 3x = 5x.

lines.say: Easy. So two baskets plus three loose apples is five x?
lines.cap: Easy. So two baskets plus three loose apples is 5x?

lines.say: No! Baskets and loose apples are different things. Two x plus three stays two x plus three.
lines.cap: No! Baskets and loose apples are different things. 2x + 3 stays 2x + 3.

lines.say: Got it. Add baskets to baskets, and apples to apples.
lines.cap: Got it. Add baskets to baskets, and apples to apples.

lines.say: Four baskets hold four x apples. If each basket holds six apples, then x is six.
lines.cap: Four baskets hold 4x apples. If each basket holds 6 apples, then x = 6.

lines.say: So four times six: twenty-four apples.
lines.cap: So 4 × 6 = 24 apples.

lines.say: Okay, Teacher. Give me a real exam question.
lines.cap: Okay, Teacher. Give me a real exam question.

lines.say: Newton picks seventeen apples. He fills three baskets, and two apples are left over. How many apples are in each basket?
lines.cap: Newton picks 17 apples. He fills 3 baskets, and 2 apples are left over. How many apples are in each basket?

lines.say: Write it down: three x plus two equals seventeen.
lines.cap: Write it down: 3x + 2 = 17.

lines.say: Take away the two loose apples: three x equals fifteen.
lines.cap: Take away the 2 loose apples: 3x = 15.

lines.say: Share fifteen between three baskets: x equals five.
lines.cap: Share 15 between 3 baskets: x = 5.

lines.say: Five apples in each basket. Check: three fives are fifteen, plus two is seventeen. Yes!
lines.cap: Five apples in each basket. Check: 3 × 5 = 15, plus 2 is 17. Yes!

lines.say: Your turn! Two x equals ten. What is x?
lines.cap: Your turn! 2x = 10. What is x?

lines.say: Five! Two baskets of five apples make ten.
lines.cap: x = 5! Two baskets of five apples make ten.

lines.say: Remember: x is just a number, waiting to be found.
lines.cap: Remember: x is just a number, waiting to be found.

lines.say: Okay. But what about at home, at nine at night, when question seven just won't work?
lines.cap: Okay. But what about at home, at nine at night, when question seven just won't work?

lines.say: That's why we built Crest Slate.
lines.cap: That's why we built Crest Slate.

lines.say: Crest Slate is Royal Crest's own maths canvas. It works on a tablet, a laptop, or a phone.
lines.cap: Crest Slate is Royal Crest's own maths canvas. It works on a tablet, a laptop, or a phone.

lines.say: Take a photo of the question, and draw a box around it. Slate reads it, right there on the page.
lines.cap: Take a photo of the question, and draw a box around it. Slate reads it, right there on the page.

lines.say: Then you choose: solve it step by step, ask for one hint at a time, or let Slate mark your own working.
lines.cap: Then you choose: solve it step by step, ask for one hint at a time, or let Slate mark your own working.

lines.say: And here's my favourite part. Slate puts the answer back into the equation, to check that it really works.
lines.cap: And here’s my favourite part: Slate puts the answer back into the equation, to check that it really works.

lines.say: Graph paper, number lines, x and y axes. Type y equals x squared, minus five x, plus six, and Slate draws the graph.
lines.cap: Graph paper, number lines, x–y axes. Type y = x² − 5x + 6, and Slate draws the graph.

lines.say: Got it wrong? Slate shows you the first slip, kindly. Seventeen minus two is fifteen, not nineteen.
lines.cap: Got it wrong? Slate shows you the first slip, kindly: 17 − 2 is 15, not 19.

lines.say: Hints come first, because we want you to think first, then check.
lines.cap: Hints come first, because we want you to think first, then check.

lines.say: It covers all nine Cambridge maths topic areas, from number and algebra to trigonometry and statistics.
lines.cap: It covers all nine Cambridge maths topic areas, from number and algebra to trigonometry and statistics.

lines.say: And it runs on Royal Crest's own A.I. model, not a public chatbot, with no adverts and no distractions.
lines.cap: And it runs on Royal Crest’s own AI model: not a public chatbot, with no adverts and no distractions.

lines.say: Crest Slate lives inside Crest Quest, our learner portal, right next to your marks, your timetable and your homework.
lines.cap: Crest Slate lives inside Crest Quest, our learner portal, right next to your marks, your timetable and your homework.

lines.say: From Newton's quill to your stylus. x is just a number, waiting to be found.
lines.cap: From Newton’s quill to your stylus. x is just a number, waiting to be found.
